question: What are the three Greek root words that make up the word epidemiology?
explanation: You've got this! The term breaks down nicely: epi means 'upon', demos means 'people', and logos means 'study'. Together, they form the study of health events affecting populations. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h1)

question: How does epidemiology differ from everyday bedside nursing care?

options.A: Epidemiology treats the entire community as the patient rather than focusing on a single individual.
options.B: Epidemiology relies solely on laboratory microscope findings instead of patient interviews.
options.C: Epidemiology ignores prevention entirely to focus only on end-stage disease management.
options.D: Epidemiology only deals with surgical complications rather than chronic illnesses.

explanation: Think of it this way: bedside nursing cares for one patient at a time, while epidemiology steps back to look at whole communities and find health patterns. Both are super important! [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h1)

question: When an epidemiologist asks where and when a disease is happening, which component are they studying?
explanation: Great try! 'Distribution' is all about mapping out the frequency and pattern of health events—looking at time, place, and who is affected. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h2)

question: What do 'determinants' represent in epidemiological studies?

options.A: The administrative rules governing public health nurses
options.B: The financial cost of treating a chronic illness in a clinic
options.C: The causes and risk factors that influence health and disease
options.D: The total number of hospital beds available in a community

explanation: Don't let the big word trip you up! Determinants are simply the underlying causes and risk factors—like germs, habits, or surroundings—that change someone's health status. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h2)

question: What are the three parts of the traditional epidemiological triad?
explanation: You will see this triad everywhere in public health! It looks at how the disease agent interacts with the vulnerable host (the person) and their surrounding environment. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h3)

question: A public health nurse hands out mosquito nets to prevent malaria. Which part of the epidemiological triad is this mainly targeting?
explanation: Spot on! Mosquito nets create a physical block between you and the environmental vector, modifying the surrounding environment where disease transmission happens. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h3)

question: Why is studying the natural history of a disease important for nurses?

options.A: It proves that environmental factors have no impact on human health.
options.B: It eliminates the need for any laboratory testing during an outbreak.
options.C: It helps nurses and doctors know what to expect at each stage of an illness.
options.D: It guarantees that pharmaceutical companies will make a profit on new drugs.

explanation: When you understand how a disease naturally progresses from start to finish, you know the best time to step in and help your patient recover! [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h4)

question: Which of the following is a primary goal of conducting epidemiological studies?

options.A: Replacing bedside clinical nurses with data entry clerks
options.B: Eliminating the need for patient consent in research trials
options.C: Providing a foundation for public health policy and disease control
options.D: Ensuring that all hospitals maintain identical financial budgets

explanation: Epidemiology isn't just about numbers—it gives health leaders the real-world evidence they need to build strong health policies and stop outbreaks. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h4)

question: How does a clinical ward nurse use epidemiological thinking during a shift?

options.A: By writing national health laws for the ministry of health
options.B: By performing complex statistical data entry for research journals
options.C: By noticing an increase in infections on the ward and looking for a common cause
options.D: By manufacturing new antibiotics in the hospital pharmacy

explanation: Everyday nurses use mini-epidemiology all the time! Whenever you notice a sudden cluster of similar infections on your ward and start searching for the source, that's epidemiological thinking. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h5)

question: A community health nurse checks local clinic records to see which neighborhoods have the highest asthma rates in children. Why is this so helpful?

options.A: To prove that childhood illnesses are impossible to prevent
options.B: To penalize local clinics that failed to cure their patients
options.C: To target prevention and education programs where they are needed most
options.D: To stop families from moving into polluted urban areas

explanation: Resources are always limited, so finding out exactly where a disease hits hardest lets nurses focus their education and support where it will do the most good. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T1#GNS313_U1_T1_h5)
